paper_title: Self-Evolving Evaluation Environments for Computer-Use Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are rapidly improving, yet their evaluation remains largely static. Existing benchmarks provide a strong foundation, but fixed difficulty ceilings, limited feature coverage, and coarse aggregate scores progressively weaken their discriminative and diagnostic value. We introduce CUA-SEE, a closed-loop evaluation environment that co-evolves tasks and executable verifiers from rollout evidence. It disentangles three objectives: benchmark evolution expands evaluation scope through cohort-calibrated difficulty and coverage growth; diagnostic evolution increases resolution through agent-conditional capability-boundary probes; and verifier evolution improves precision by translating changing requirements into state-grounded checkpoints with adversarial validation. Across multiple agents, applications, and rounds, CUA-SEE generates challenging, measurable tasks while preserving process-level evidence. Our results position adaptive evaluation as a scalable counterpart to self-evolving agents, continuously tracking what agents can do, where their boundaries lie, and how reliably progress is measured.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are rapidly improving, yet their evaluation remains largely static. Existing benchmarks provide strong foundation, but fixed difficulty ceilings, limited feature coverage, and coarse aggregate scores progressively weaken their discriminative and diagnostic value. We introduce CUA-SEE, closed-loop evaluation environment that co-evolves tasks and executable verifiers from rollout evidence. It disentangles three objectives: benchmark evolution expands evaluation scope through cohort-calibrated difficulty and coverage growth; diagnostic evolution increases resolution through agentconditional capability-boundary probes; and verifier evolution improves precision by translating changing requirements into state-grounded checkpoints with adversarial validation. Across multiple agents, applications, and rounds, CUA-SEE generates challenging, measurable tasks while preserving process-level evidence. Our results position adaptive evaluation as scalable counterpart to evolving CUAs, continuously tracking what agents can do, where their boundaries lie, and how reliably progress is measured. 1. Introduction Agent evaluation, which underpins both scientific progress and real-world deployment, has long been fundamentally yet challenging problem [6, 11, 14, 21]. For computer-use agents (CUAs) [8, 10, 19, 23], evaluation is harder because success must be verified against intricate software-specific states and multifaceted task requirements, rather than textual responses (e.g., search agents [2, 7, 9]) or binary execution results (e.g., code agents [5]). Current benchmarks [18, 20] have established an essential foundation for CUA evaluation by manually curating realistic tasks and taskspecific verifiers. However, this human-authored, one-shot construction paradigm is costly to scale and renders both tasks and verifiers largely fixed as agent capabilities evolve, giving rise to several critical limitations [4, 17, 22]. This static paradigm creates three consequential limitations: (1) fixed task set imposes difficulty ceiling: once agents master its tasks, scores saturate and cease to distinguish further progress. (2) Manual construction provides limited feature coverage; in our audit of core OSWorld applications, the existing tasks exercise less than 20% of the available software-feature taxonomy. (3) Static benchmarks lack evaluation dynamics: they neither track moving capability boundary nor actively search for newly emerging weaknesses, shortcut behaviors, and generalization gaps. These limitations reveal the necessity of an evaluation system that evolves in tandem with the LLM agents it assesses. To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose CUA-SEE, Self-Evolving Evaluation environment for computer-use agents. CUA-SEE reconceptualizes evaluation as dynamic, closed-loop process where tasks, executable verifiers, and agent rollout evidence continuously inform and refine one another. At each round, agents interact with the current task-verifier pairs; validity-filtered trajectories and checkpoint outcomes update the measurement state; and this evidence determines what tasks should be measured in the next round and how the corresponding verifiers should be implemented. Specifically, our framework is designed around three core components that work in concert to disentangle three dimensions often conflated in conventional task-hardening pipelines: evaluation scope, diagnostic resolution, and measurement precision. Scope. To address the fixed difficulty ceiling and feature coverage, we expand the evaluation scope of static benchmarks by introducing an evolution operator, called Benchmark Task Evolution, which constructs shared, modelneutral benchmark from aligned trajectories of heterogeneous agent cohort. It retains all replicates, separates execution validity from task success, and uses cohort agreement and disagreement to calibrate whether source task is mastered, discriminating, unstable, or confounded. Evolution then optimizes two suite-level objectives: advancing the measurable difficulty frontier and expanding coverage 1 Table 1. Comparison of evolvable properties.

Candidate descendants may increase precision, scale, state dependence, procedure depth, feature composition, or add previously uncovered but coherent operation. Each descendant preserves semantic lineage anchor and must introduce explicit, independently observable measurement obligations, while round-level registry coordinates coverage growth across tasks. Benchmark evolution thus broadens what the suite can measure without tailoring the benchmark to an idiosyncratic failure of one agent. Resolution. The second operator, called Diagnostic Task Evolution, is agent-conditional and concentrates evaluation budget near uncertain capability boundaries. batch-level planner aggregates longitudinal evidence into capability, software, and feature maps to dispatch targeted experiments over seven calibrated dimensions such as precision control and state-dependent reasoning, as detailed in Appendix A. The task-level evolver realizes each experiment as natural task with one primary dimension at controlled intensity. The search is adaptive rather than monotonically harder: Clean successes and failures prompt upward and downward probes, respectively; partial or censored runs trigger deconfounding. This adaptive bracketing refines where an agents pass-fail transition lies, turning coarse benchmark scores into locally attributable capability evidence. Precision. Both task operators share requirementpreserving measurement backbone, termed as Verifier Evolution. The third component uses task-agnostic software adapters to probe native state-export surfaces and normalize them into shared CanonicalState schema. Over this substrate, an information-isolated verifier agent generates atomic requirement-level checkpoints while pass agent independently realizes valid completion state; their adversarial cross-review improves checkpoint completeness and PRE/PASS discrimination [12, 16]. Verifier evolution thus determines how faithfully evolving agent behavior is measured while exposing process-level signals for diagnosis and future dense-feedback learning. Extensive experiments across five SOTA agents demonstrate that CUA-SEE continuously restores evaluation informativeness. Over four evolution rounds, the macro-average agent score decreases from 60.6 to 47.5 while trajectory length increases from 27.4 to 39.3 steps, and exact feature coverage expands by 3.65. Beyond producing harder and broader tasks, CUA-SEE adaptively concentrates diagnostic probes near each agents capability boundary, revealing agent-specific and software-specific weaknesses obscured by aggregate scores. Meanwhile, the evolved checkpoint verifiers achieve 84.0% agreement with human trajectory judgments. To summarize, our main contributions are: 1. We formulate self-evolving evaluation for CUAs as closed loop in which task demand, measurement instruments, and validity-filtered rollout evidence are updated jointly across rounds, addressing the mismatch between continually improving agents and static benchmarks. 2. We introduce two complementary task-evolution operators: cohort-grounded benchmark operator that expands evaluation scope through measurable frontier and feature-coverage growth, and an agent-conditional diagnostic operator that increases resolution through controlled, adaptive capability-boundary probes. 3. We develop requirement-preserving verifier evolution pipeline that improves measurement precision by converting evolved task obligations into executable, stategrounded checkpoints, enabling validity-aware capability estimation and richer process supervision than terminal scalar rewards alone. 2. Related Work CUA Environments & Benchmarks. While popular benchmarks like OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena [1, 15, 18] offer robust, reproducible evaluation of computer-use agents in real desktop environments, they are limited to fixed set of pre-curated tasks. As agent capability improves, extending such benchmarks by hand is costly, difficult to scale, and slow to expose new capability limits. Recent systems automate parts of this process: CUA-Gym [12] generates verifiable task-state-reward tuples, while OpenCom2 Figure 3. System overview. CUA-SEE forms closed loop of task evolution, verifier evolution, and agent-environment rollout, as summarized by the central workflow. The left panel details task evolution: rollout evidence is first aggregated at the batch level to plan the next round, followed by two complementary forms of per-task evolution: benchmark evolution for population-level measurement growth and diagnostic evolution for agent-conditional boundary refinement. The right panel presents verifier evolution, which progressively translates evolved task requirements into grounded, executable, and rigorously validated measurements. The bottom panel shows the shared substrate that supports all stages of the evaluation loop, expanding the 8 OSWorld applications to 20 verifiable desktop environments. puter [16] builds tasks with state verifiers and partial-credit rewards. Their main goal, however, is to scale verifiable environments or training data rather than repeatedly adapt benchmark to the observed behavior of fixed agent. Evaluation Evolution. Early efforts have begun to explore benchmark evolution through rule-based editing, scheduled data refreshes, and agent-driven exploration [6, 13, 17]. AutoEvoEval applies predefined transformations to reasoning or question-answering tasks, while EvoCodeBench periodically adds new code tasks. Most closely related, TRACE [3] uses test-time exploration to generate progressively harder web-search tasks and verify their solutions for reproducibility. Unlike our approach, however, TRACEs scope is limited to task difficulty, and it leaves the critical role of verifier evolution unaddressed by employing static, exact-match verifier. 3. Methodology As depicted in Figure 3, CUA-SEE is designed to co-evolve tasks and verifiers through closed loop fueled by evidence from agent-environment rollouts. 3.1. Scope: Benchmark Task Evolution Benchmark task evolution expands the population-level scope of evaluation. Given source tasks, aligned trajectories from heterogeneous agent cohort, and the accumulated coverage registry, it produces model-neutral batch of task descendants that advances the measurable difficulty frontier and enlarges the set of capabilities and software operations covered by the benchmark. Aligned Multi-Agent Evidence. We join trajectories by canonical source-task identity and retain every compatible 3 (a) Benchmark evolution using the Chrome privacy task. (b) Diagnosing Kimi using the LibreOffice Calc pivot-table task. Figure 4. Case studies of benchmark evolution and diagnostic evolution. More examples and results are attached in the Appendix. replicate. Evidence integrity is modeled independently of task outcome: valid successes and failures provide clean evidence, step-limit runs are retained as censored observations, and setup, controller, or environment failures are marked as invalid. Using scores, termination states, checkpoint transitions, regressions, and path diversity, we classify each source lineage as universally easy, mostly mastered, discriminating, universally hard, unstable, or confounded. This cohort-level state determines the admissible strength of evolution while preventing transient or model-specific errors from becoming benchmark objectives. Bi-Objective Round Planning. Evolution jointly optimizes difficulty-frontier and feature-coverage growth at the round level. Difficulty growth requires measurable increase in one or more calibrated capability demands without material regression of the overall task, whereas coverage growth requires strict set addition on either the exact software-taxonomy-operation surface or the capabilityintensity surface. Required action families are tracked separately as exposure rather than treated as agent capabilities. shared lineage and coverage registry coordinates parallel workers and prevents repeated references to an already measured feature from being counted as new breadth. Individual tasks may specialize in difficulty or coverage, but the selected batch must advance both objectives in aggregate. dently measurable demand or coverage cell. Candidates may increase precision, dependence, procedural depth, or verification requirements, but unrelated feature grafts and superficial elaboration do not constitute evolution. Candidate Selection Gates. candidate is eligible only if it preserves the lineage anchor, avoids material difficulty regression, remains feasible within the interaction budget, admits uniquely observable final state, and is justified by model-neutral evidence. Eligible candidates are ranked by feasibility, verifiability, calibrated difficulty, coverage gain, model neutrality, and naturalness; step requirements above 0.85 of the available budget are rejected. The output remains general benchmark task proposal until every evolved obligation is instantiated by an executable verifier. 3.2. Resolution: Diagnostic Task Evolution Diagnostic task evolution increases the resolution of evaluation around an individual agents capability boundary. This multi-agent system follows hierarchical process: batchlevel planner converts longitudinal rollout evidence into agent-specific diagnostic dispatches, and per-task evolver realizes each dispatch as controlled task proposal. The objective is not maximal difficulty or scope (i.e., Benchmark Evolution), but locally attributable observation that narrows the agents pass-fail boundary. Lineage-Anchored Evolution Directions. For each eligible source, we construct candidates with four directions: difficulty escalation, coverage expansion, transfer with measurable escalation, and their coherent combination. Every candidate preserves lineage anchor, the semantic demand that makes cross-round comparison meaningful, while allowing values, targets, scale, context, and supporting subgoals to change. Purely horizontal transfer is excluded: transferred task must introduce an indepenTarget Diagnostic Cell. To allocate well-targeted dispatches, the batch planner first separates pass, partial, confounded, and invalid outcomes, using only observations with valid setup and verifiers as clean boundary evidence. It then aggregates multiple analytical views to identify stable, failing, or insufficiently supported regions. Each dispatch targets diagnostic cell defined by software, feature, primary capability, and intensity, together with control dimensions and confound limits. Priority is given to decon4 founding blocked evidence, resolving uncertain transitions, testing transfer of suspected weaknesses, expanding undersupported cells, and replicating non-monotonic results. preservation conditions, and prohibited side effects are retained as first-class obligations rather than silently omitted or merged into coarse success criteria. KNN-Inspired Evolution Candidate Realization. For one dispatched source lineage, the task evolver constructs local neighborhood of candidates: the requested intensity, cleaner lower-intensity fallback, and, when feasible, an adjacent higher-intensity or alternate-factor probe. Each task is defined by primary demand dimension and several secondary dimensions, all drawn from the 7D capabilities: scale consistency, precision control, target grounding, state-dependent reasoning, procedure following, feature integration, or verification and control. Intensities are scored from 0 to 5 using dimension-specific factors derived from the instruction, initial state, and verifier obligations; they describe task demand rather than predicted agent performance (detailed in Appendix A). Adaptive Probe Policy. The probe direction is evidencedriven rather than assumed to be monotonically upward. Clean passes or failures adjust intensity upward or downward, respectively, while ambiguous results trigger corrective actions like deconfounding, simplification, or replication. Each proposal records expected failure modes and explicit verifier requirements, and it updates the agents capability boundary only after verifier evolution and valid rollout make the resulting evidence eligible. Confound-Controlled Candidate Selection. Capability demand is factorized from nuisance variables including step budget, context load and verifier risk. Candidates that violate dispatch limits, exceed the step budget, or lack an observable outcome are redesigned or rejected. Remaining ones are ranked by dispatch alignment, diagnostic cleanliness, secondary coverage value, etc. This criterion deliberately favors slightly weaker but cleanly attributable probe over harder task which cannot resolve agent boundaries. 3.3. Precision: Unified Verifier Evolution Verifier evolution co-evolves the measurement instrument with each task so that increased task demand remains faithfully observable. The objective is to maximize coverage of the evolved task contract while preserving verifier lineage, grounding every check in observable state, and explicitly representing verification gaps. Requirement-Centric Contract Decomposition. We reconstruct the evolved task contract as set of independently testable outcome requirements derived from the explicit evaluator requirements and atomic clauses of the instruction. Target values, ordering constraints, artifact states, State Grounding and Observability. Each requirement maps to an observable state field or artifact, planned checkpoint, and one of three coverage states: covered, partially observable, or unverifiable. State paths must be supported by the applications state catalog or captured snapshots; proxy checks based only on file existence, filenames, setup state, or unavailable pre-action values are disallowed. Unsupported clauses remain explicit coverage gaps rather than unsound surrogates, avoiding selection bias against complex, harder-to-inspect applications that discarding such tasks would introduce. Checkpoint-Lineage Transformation. Given the source verifier, each existing checkpoint receives an explicit lineage operation: KEEP for an unchanged obligation, MODIFY for changed target or expected value, and REMOVE for an obligation absent from the evolved task; ADD introduces checkpoints for newly required effects. The original OSWorld evaluator may provide semantic evidence about intended facts, tolerances, and conjunction structure, but the evolved task contract remains authoritative. Optional trajectories and checkpoint histories are used to confirm state paths and expose regressions, while an individual failed rollout is not treated as sufficient evidence of verifier error. Executable Verifier Construction. To construct verifier, each software is equipped with task-agnostic adapter that probes native state-export interfaces (e.g., debug protocols) to extract and normalize its snapshot into shared CanonicalState schema. The transformed contract is compiled into distinct schema-grounded checkpoints, each of which checks one task effect and returns specific expected-versus-actual reason. Every requirement must map to checkpoint or be declared as an explicit observability gap, prohibiting shortcuts like unconditional passes or inference-based fallbacks. partially observable task remains rollout-ready when at least one meaningful target effect is soundly verified and all omissions are declared. Validation and Adversarial Audit. Validation separates three static gates (i.e., syntax and imports, structural contract, and static schema), from two behavioral gates (i.e., PRE/PASS discrimination and checkpoint-wise negative fixtures). An information-isolated pass agent independently realizes an executable PASS state and audits checkpoint necessity and completeness, while verifier agent audits whether that state genuinely satisfies the task without access to the pass implementation. Revisions are adopted only when they preserve task semantics and do not reduce the best validated verifier score. 4. Experiments (More Results in Appendix) Experimental Setups. While CUA-SEEs substrate spans 20 applications (Appendix B.1), we track the eight core OSWorld apps under 50-step budget for strict R0 alignment, reporting normalized scores, steps, and tokens. For benchmark evolution, 100 lineage-aligned task groups evolve from R0 through R1R4 across five SOTA agents (2,500 paired observations controlling sample drift in total): Kimi-K2.6, Seed-2.1-Pro, and Gemini-3.5-Flash drive evolution, while Qwen-3.7-Plus and GPT-5.5 are strictly held out. For diagnostic evolution, independent boundary probes are generated over the seven 0-5 capability dimensions (Section 3.2) for Gemini, Kimi, and Seed. R0 uses native OSWorld tasks and verifiers; evolved rounds use CanonicalState verifiers. Scoring and Metrics. Benchmark scores average normalized episode scores to retain partial credit. Diagnostic outcomes separate valid pass ([0.99, 1]), partial ((0.01, 0.99)), and fail ([0, 0.01]) runs from 50-step censored and confounded/invalid runs; matrix values report task-weighted checkpoint means over eligible clean episodes rather than full-task pass rates or averages of round means (gray cells denote unavailable evidence). 4.1. Evaluations on Evolved Benchmarks Higher Task Difficulty. As summarized in Table 2, we conclude the following: (1) The evolved benchmark becomes substantially more demanding. Across all five agents, the macro-average score decreases from 60.6 in R1 to 47.5 in R4, while the average trajectory length increases from 27.4 to 39.3 steps. (2) Kimi, Qwen, and GPT obtain 6 (a) Proportions of primary capability evaluated. (b) Intensity distributions across capabilities. (c) Average capability demand across software applications. Colors denote mean checkpoint scores; gray cells indicate unavailable evidence. Figure 7. Round-wise benchmark evolution. Later rounds are harder and provide broader cumulative coverage. slightly higher scores in R2 than in R1; nevertheless, their trajectory lengths increase by 9.5, 4.6, and 5.8 steps, respectively. This indicates that later tasks generally require longer interaction chains, while newly introduced features may align better with the capabilities of particular agents. (3) Difficulty growth is uneven across applications. Chrome remains comparatively easy in later rounds, whereas GIMP, Calc, and Writer exhibit larger score reductions. Broader Feature Coverage. Feature coverage is organized hierarchically from broad feature families, through finer-grained feature categories, to exact executable feature operations within each software. (1) The results in Table 3 also demonstrate consistent and hierarchical expansion of functional coverage across successive evolution rounds, with steady growth in feature families and categories and 3.65 increase in exact feature operations by R4. (2) These gains appear across all eight applications, indicating that evolution broadens the benchmark as whole rather than concentrating on few software domains. Overall, these results confirm that iterative benchmark evolution systematically broadens the functional and operational scope of the benchmark rather than merely rephrasing existing tasks. Multi-Faceted Task Statistics. Beyond difficulty and coverage metrics, the evolved tasks exhibit rich, multifaceted structure, with detailed statistics shown in Fig- (1) The tasks exhibit compound capability deure 5. mands, with procedure following and target grounding fre- (2) Caquently required at moderate-to-high intensities. pability profiles vary substantially across applicationsfor example, Calc emphasizes precision control, whereas Chrome and VLC place greater demands on target groundingdemonstrating software-specific rather than templated difficulty. the suite covers diverse interaction families, spanning clicks, text, keyboard shortcuts, and long-tail operations such as scrolling and dragging. (3) Finally, 4.2. Evolved Diagnoses of Specific Agents Effective and Discriminative Diagnosis. (1) Figure 2 reveals that our Diagnostic Evolution continually mines the agents pass/fail boundary, thereby shifting the original saturated benchmark from near-universal success toward more informative regime where nuanced diagnosis becomes possible. (2) Our method diagnoses heterogeneous capabilities and distinct software-specific strengths that are typically obscured by aggregate scores. As visualized in Figure 6 and Supplementary Figures 13j and 13f, this analysis reveals unique performance signatures for each agent across various diagnostic matrices, such as capability-intensity and software-feature. (3) Successive rounds expand coverage across capability, software, function, and action dimensions. Each round consistently introduces 5773 new feature leaves, ensuring that our diagnosis grows in breadth and is not merely resampling similar challenges. 7 (a) Checkpoint distribution (b) Software profile (c) Requirement coverage (d) Requirement alignment Figure 8. Verifier construction statistics on the Kimi diagnostic benchmark across checkpoint-count distribution, software-specific checkpoint profile, atomic requirement coverage, and checkpointrequirement alignment (Gemini and Seed in Supplementary Figure 12). Figure 9. Binary agreement between human judgments and verifier outcomes. Figure 10. Token composition and API-equivalent cost per successful artifact. Agent-Specific Diagnostic Profiles. Based on the diagnosis, we construct specific agent profiles. (1) Capability: Gemini is strong in precision control and target grounding, but high-scale consistency remains challenging. (2) Operation: Kimi is reliable on clicking, typing, and navigation, while Seed is more sensitive to dragging, scrolling, and state-dependent controls. (3) Feature: Kimi shows the most consistent feature-level performance, whereas Seed varies more across document and media features. (4) Software: All three agents are more stable in Chrome and VS Code, while GIMP and Thunderbird expose clearer weaknesses. 4.3. Validation of Evolved Verifiers Trajectory-Level Verifier Agreement. We manually assess convergent validity on 400 Kimi trajectories across four evolution rounds in Figure 9. Human judgments and checkpoint verifiers agree on 84.0% of runs (Cohens κ = 0.640), with agreement increasing from 81% to 89%. Continuous scores also show moderate concordance. Audited disagreements mainly arise from incomplete adapter state, partial verifier coverage, and state-field mismatches, highlighting the remaining observability limitations. native-adapter limits (e.g., Thunderbird). Moreover, checkpoint counts track requirement counts along the = diagonal (r = 0.550.65), with PARTIAL tasks still grounding 37 checkpoints; the independent trajectory audit (Figure 9) further validates behavioral precision. 4.4. Evaluation Reliability and Evolution Efficiency Evaluation Reliability. Under live-VM budget and native observability limits, cross-round and cross-agent comparisons remain fair and discriminative: (1) Out-of-cohort generalization: held-out Qwen (26.9) and GPT (24.0) match the cohorts difficulty progression without driving evolution. (2) Calibrated co-evolution: KEEP/MODIFY inheritance, isolated PASS-state solvability gates, rising human agreement (81% to 89%), verifier-independent 2 step, and 23.5 token growth rule out verifier drift. (3) Partial-verifier symmetry: retaining sound PARTIAL verifiers preserves hard-to-inspect apps while applying identical checks across all agents without artificial score deflation. (4) Structured discrimination: while low R4 pass rates (1319%) narrow the macro spread, continuous scores lift boundary informativeness (+20.8 pp to 69.7) and expose 2037 pp per-app rank reversals masked by scalar means. Evolution Efficiency. In Figure 10, we measure the token usage and API-equivalent cost of successful task and verifier evolution runs, aggregated across rounds for three diagnostic agents and the multi-agent benchmark. Costs are estimated from cached input, uncached input, and output tokens using GPT-5.5 API rates. Verifier evolution exhibits stable costs across agents, while benchmark task evolution is more expensive due to its larger shared context, indicating that context constructionnot verifier generationis the primary efficiency bottleneck. Verifier Statistics. Figure 8 and Supplementary Figure 12 confirm that evolved verifiers stay tightly aligned with growing task contracts rather than collapsing into minimal checks. Across 962 tasks (4.82 checkpoints/task), atomic requirement coverage reaches 92.5% overallexceeding 85% in nearly all apps, with lower coverage isolated to 5. Conclusion We present CUA-SEE, closed-loop evaluation framework that co-evolves tasks and executable verifiers from computer-use agent trajectories. Benchmark evolution expands difficulty and coverage, diagnostic evolution probes 8 agent-conditional capability boundaries, and verifier evolution grounds changing requirements in audited checkpoints. Experiments across agents, applications, and rounds show that adaptive evaluation remains informative beyond static benchmarks while producing attributable capability evidence. These results establish evolving evaluation as practical counterpart to increasingly capable, self-evolving agents.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: Large language models were used during this project for manuscript language polishing, figure and layout drafting, and AI-assisted software engineering (vibe coding) of evaluation, data-processing, and visualization scripts. In addition, LLM and VLM inference APIs serve as core runtime components within the CUA-SEE synthesis pipeline and the evaluated computer-use agent rollouts, as detailed in Section 3 and Appendix B.2. All methodological designs, code implementations, experimental results, and scientific claims were inspected and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the contents of this paper.

sections.title: System Boundary
sections.content: This section defines the foundational taxonomies, ordinal capability rubrics, and invariance boundaries that anchor CUA-SEE across evolution rounds. Feature Taxonomy. As illustrated in Figure 11, we organize the feature space as four-level hierarchy spanning software, feature families, functional categories, and concrete operations. The representative branches illustrate how application-level functionality is decomposed into directly executable and verifiable actions across browsers, productivity tools, creative applications, diagram editors, and media players. This structured taxonomy provides consistent basis for measuring feature coverage, identifying underexplored functionality, and guiding task evolution toward broader and more diverse interaction capabilities. Capability Dimensions and Intensity Rubric. Independent of software features, task demand is parameterized over seven orthogonal capability dimensions scored on an ordinal 05 rubric  (Table 4)  . Scores are anchored in objective task factorssuch as target count, value coupling, distractor similarity, state-derivation depth, and dependency chain lengthderived strictly from the instruction, initial state, and verifier contract rather than predicted agent performance. To keep capability probes attributable, nuisance confounds (step-budget ratio, context load, navigation hiddenness, and verifier risk) are tracked separately and bounded during candidate selection. Action-Family Exposure Taxonomy. To characterize low-level GUI interaction demands without conflating them with cognitive capabilities, each evolved profile records required exposure over eight canonical action families: click, text entry, keyboard shortcut, menu navigation, dialog entry, numeric-widget manipulation, drag, and scroll. Action annotations represent task-required interaction exposure rather than trajectory-inferred behavior, ensuring that softwareaction profiles remain well-defined even when an agent fails early or chooses an alternative UI path. 1 Figure 11. Feature taxonomy hierarchy tree. Software functionality is organized into four levelsfeature family, category, and concrete operation beneath each applicationwith representative branches shown for diverse software. The feature-, family- , category-, and operation-level coverage metrics reported in the main text are computed over this hierarchy. Fixed Substrate vs. Self-Evolving Artifacts. To clarify what self-evolving entails and why cross-round comparison remains stable, Table 5 separates CUA-SEEs invariant infrastructure from its round-wise generated artifacts. Holding the VM substrate, native state adapters, taxonomies, scoring rubrics, and validation gates fixed ensures that changes across rounds reflect genuine growth in task Table 4. Seven calibrated capability dimensions, grounded task factors, and condensed 05 ordinal intensity anchors.

B. Experiment Details and Prompts B.1. Experimental Setup Evaluation scope. We evaluate benchmark evolution and diagnostic evolution on realistic Ubuntu desktop environments derived from OSWorld. As shown in Figure 1 and Figure 3, CUA-SEEs shared measurement substrate expands the eight core OSWorld applications (Chrome, GIMP, LibreOffice Calc, LibreOffice Impress, LibreOffice Writer, Thunderbird, VLC, and Visual Studio Code) with twelve additional native-CanonicalState-instrumented desktop environmentsBlender, VSCodium, JupyterLab, Krita, Draw.io, SMPlayer, OBS Studio, ONLYOFFICE, OpenScreen, ComfyUI, Zotero, and Bravebringing total software breadth to 20 applications across browsers, office suites, IDEs, creative/3D studios, diagramming, media production, and research workflows. To ensure strict tasklineage correspondence with the original R0 benchmark without confounding cross-round metrics with newly introduced software domains, the longitudinal multi-round panel (R0R4) and diagnostic matrices (R0R3) track the eight core OSWorld applications, while the full 20application substrate supports broader benchmark synthesis and scope expansion. Benchmark evolution is evaluated on heterogeneous panel of five computer-use agents: KimiK2.6, Seed-2.1-Pro, Gemini-3.5-Flash, Qwen-3.7-Plus, and GPT-5.5. Diagnostic evolution focuses on three representative agentsKimi-K2.6, Seed-2.1-Pro, and Gemini-3.5Flashbecause it constructs separate, agent-conditional task sequence for each target agent. Benchmark-evolution protocol. We start from fixed panel of 100 OSWorld task lineages and evolve each lineage for four rounds, producing the original benchmark R0 and evolved suites R1R4. Every round retains the same 100 lineage identifiers and is evaluated by all five agents, yielding 500 taskagent observations per round and 2,500 observations over the complete trajectory. This paired design prevents changes in aggregate performance from being attributed to changing task sample. Each evolved task is also annotated with seven-dimensional capability-demand vector on 05 scale and with exact softwaretaxonomy operation cells, enabling difficulty and coverage to be measured independently. Diagnostic-evolution protocol. Diagnostic evolution is run independently for each target agent. The current experiment contains four 100-task rounds for Kimi and three 100-task rounds each for Seed and Gemini, for total of 1,000 evolved task profiles. The primary diagnostic matrices pool matched 100-task R0 baseline with R1R3 for each agent, yielding 1,200 planned agenttaskround slots before rollout availability and validity filtering. Kimi R4 is included only in task-generation and verifier analyses because it is outside the R0R3 matrix scope. Profiles without eligible rollouts are retained as missing or unavailable evidence rather than imputed as failure. Rollout parameters. Each episode is limited to 50 environment-interaction steps. The environment records the complete action trajectory, the terminal normalized task score, and state-hook checkpoint traces. We classify scores of at least 0.99 as pass and scores of at most 0.01 as fail; in2 Table 5. Lifecycle boundary separating fixed evaluation infrastructure from round-wise self-evolving artifacts in CUA-SEE.

B.2. Implementation Compute and deployment. Task synthesis, verifier construction, and result aggregation are executed on two CPU servers. The primary OSW server runs Ubuntu 22.04 with 96 Intel Xeon Platinum 8163 vCPUs and 376 GiB RAM; the auxiliary SCI server runs Ubuntu 20.04 with 256 AMD EPYC 7T83 vCPUs and 1008 GiB RAM. Neither server uses local GPU because model inference is provided by remote Codex subscription or API services. Thus, capability rubrics, admissible evolution operators, confound limits, output schemas, and validation gates remain fixed across parallel workers and rounds. 4 (a) Round-R1 diagnostic evolution for Kimi, strengthening mastered VS Code replacement task into controlled scale-consistency probe. Each transition uses the preceding rollout outcome to strengthen mastered task, remove confounding requirements, or refine an uncertain capability boundary. Concurrent orchestration. Batch analysis is performed once before each diagnostic round, after which independent task workers consume the resulting dispatch.jsonl in parallel. Benchmark tasks and task-specific verifiers are parallelized similarly, while shared feature and capability registries use atomic claims to prevent duplicated coverage gains. The reusable runners default to three concurrent Codex workers, two-second launch stagger, 45minute per-task timeout, and resumable execution that skips already validated terminal artifacts; bounded repair and verifier jobs may raise concurrency to ten. Machine-readable run summaries record task status, duration, token usage, retries, validation errors, and the exact output directory. Hybrid Codex backends. We use GPT-5.5 for task and verifier synthesis and explicitly set reasoning effort to high for the reported runs. Workloads are distributed across two isolated execution modes: ChatGPT/Codex subscription backend authenticated through persistent CODEX HOME, and an API backend using an OpenAI-compatible Responses interface through Routify. worker uses exactly one backend; credentials and provider-specific environment variables from the other backend are removed, and there is no silent cross-backend fallback. This hybrid deployment allows subscription and API capacity to be combined at the campaign level without changing the skill, prompt contract, model identifier, or output schema. 5 Validation and provenance. Task workers must produce structured task, capability-profile, analysis, and task-card artifacts, all of which pass schema and semantic consistency checks before entering round. Verifier workers additionally run syntax, interface-contract, schema-grounding, PRE/PASS discrimination, and negative-fixture checks before task is marked rollout-ready. Source identifiers, lineage operations, model/backend settings, token accounting, and rollout paths are preserved in machine-readable summaries. This artifact-first design makes every plotted value traceable to task profile, one selected rollout, and one validated verifier. 1T 1 (cid:80) B.3. Metrics Normalized task score and pass rate. These pairscaled bars must therefore not be compared vertically with percentage-valued metrics. Validity-aware diagnostic outcomes. Diagnostic observations are assigned one of six mutually exclusive classes. Pass, partial, and fail correspond to scores in [0.99, 1], (0.01, 0.99), and [0, 0.01], respectively, provided the task and verifier are valid. Censored denotes zero-score run that exhausts the step budget; confounded denotes profile with blocking nuisance factor; and invalid denotes missing scores, infeasible profiles, invalid setup, or missing/unready verifier. Rows are the seven capability dimensions and columns are task-demand intensities 15. task contributes to its primary dimension and to every supporting dimension with positive recorded intensity. Thus, cell answers the question How well did the agent perform on tasks that required capability at intensity z? It does not estimate the causal effect of increasing intensity, because tasks in adjacent columns may differ in software, feature, and lineage. Intensity zero is omitted because it denotes no meaningful demand on that dimension. Softwarecapability matrix. Rows are applications and columns are capability dimensions. task contributes to every positive capability demand recorded in its profile, using the same primary/supporting attribution rule as the capabilityintensity matrix. The value therefore summarizes performance on tasks coupling particular application with particular capability demand. It is not softwareonly score and does not imply that failures are uniquely caused by that capability. Softwarefeature matrix. Each row is an application and each cell corresponds to one top-level taxonomy feature family required by at least one profile. All required features are included, with primary and supporting roles weighted equally; leaf operations are collapsed to the top-level family only for readability. The printed percentage is the rounded mean checkpoint score over clean tasks exposing that softwarefamily pair. task requiring multiple feature families contributes its episode score to each corresponding cell. 7 Softwareaction matrix. Columns represent required interaction families such as click, type, shortcut, menu navigation, dialog entry, numeric-widget manipulation, drag, and scroll. The matrix records planned action exposure from the task profile, not actions inferred from trajectory. Its color is the mean whole-task checkpoint score for tasks requiring that action family; it is therefore not an actionlocalized success rate. One task may contribute to several action columns, and R0 contributes no action cells because the original tasks do not have compatible action-exposure annotations. Missing cells and evidence maturity. In the compact paper matrices, gray cell means that no eligible clean score is available; it may be genuinely unexposed or may have planned profiles whose rollouts are censored, confounded, invalid, or missing. The annotated companion plots separate these cases: is the number of designed profiles assigned to cell, is the number of clean rollout observations, gray denotes = 0, and light blue denotes > 0 but = 0. We additionally report three coverage layers. Exposed means that at least one task profile occupies the cell, valid means that at least one clean observation occupies it, and well-sampled requires at least three clean observations drawn from at least two distinct base-task families. Matched R0 reconstruction. The original OSWorld tasks were not authored with diagnostic primary-dimension or action labels. For each agent, the R0 capability axis is reconstructed from the one-to-one R1 profile: we use the dimension selected as the R1 primary probe and that tasks recorded source-demand intensity. The full source-demand vector supplies supporting dimensions, while feature cells come from the curated R0 taxonomy sidecar. This produces matched baseline with one observation per lineage, but it should not be interpreted as an independently annotated R0 diagnostic plan. No R0 action matrix is reconstructed. Diagnostic-resolution metrics. The separate diagnosticresolution plots use manual task-level judgments and explicitly exclude checkpoint scores. Only judgments marked eligible for capability analysis are included. Boundaryregion density is the fraction of scores strictly between 20 and 80. Upward-probe transition yield is the fraction of clean-pass source tasks whose higher-intensity successors become partial or fail. strict empirical boundary bracket occurs when an upward probe changes pass to partial/fail or downward probe changes partial/fail to pass; bracket width is the absolute difference between the two capability intensities, and width-one event localizes the boundary to adjacent levels. These quantities evaluate adaptive resolution rather than overall task difficulty. Verifier metrics. Requirement coverage is the number of atomic task requirements grounded in executable checkpoints divided by the total number of extracted requirements. FULL verifier covers every requirement, whereas PARTIAL verifier preserves nonempty sound observable subset and records the remaining gaps; BLOCKED tasks have no meaningful observable checkpoint and are not rolled out. Checkpoint count is the number of callable checkpoint functions and is reported both as total and as per-task mean. READY indicates that the verifier passed syntax, interface-contract, schema-grounding, and static validation gates; it is an implementation-validity status, while empirical PRE/PASS and negative-fixture tests provide the behavioral discrimination evidence. Uncertainty estimates. For paired R0R4 benchmark comparisons, confidence intervals are obtained by 5,000 Intervals for changes retask-level bootstrap resamples. sample paired per-task differences, preserving lineage correspondence across rounds. Diagnostic matrices report cell means together with evidence counts or evidence-maturity layers rather than confidence intervals because many cells are intentionally sparse during adaptive exploration. sections.title: ROLE
sections.content: You are computer-use agent. Given task instruction, the current visual observation, and the preceding interaction history, produce the next executable action block that advances the task in the desktop environment. TASK : User-facing instruction & target state. OBSERVATION ot: Current screenshot & UI context. HISTORY ht: Prior observations & executed actions.

sections.content: 1. Ground the next action in (I, ot, ht); do not assume an unobserved interface state. 2. Emit an executable model-native action block at Am (e.g., click, drag, scroll, type, hotkey, wait, or an enabled GUI/CLI program). 3. If repeated execution leaves the screen unchanged, revise the action or choose an alternative interaction path.
